speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. The question of privilege relates to the publication in the Ottawa Evening Citizen of yesterday, March 1, 1948, of what purports to be a series of quotations from a letter which Mr. George A. Drew addressed to me on July 11, 1942, respecting the Hong Kong inquiry.
The press report, apart from other allegations, contains certain statements respecting myself as Prime Minister which are not in accord with the facts. With respect to Hong Kong, it is in effect alleged that after the government of Japan changed on October 16, 1941, and before the expedition sailed on October 27, I received messages from the United Kingdom government in the nature of the most complete warning of the probability of early hostilities. Not only is such a statement not correct, but the fact is that both before and after the expedition sailed and, indeed, until the very eve of the Japanese attack, such information as I received from the British authorities was to the effect that an early attack upon Hong Kong was not anticipated.
In my opinion, such information as the Canadian government received, at the time, from the British authorities is in complete accord with the finding of the commissioner, Chief Justice Duff, in his report, namely, that "the best informed opinion available to the Canadian authorities was that hostilities would not arise in the near future."

speechtext:
['Mr. Speaker, I hope the hon. gentleman who has preceded me will forgive me if I do not follow his remarks. However, I wish to congratulate him upon having put up a splendid fight against his adversaries and upon having put at least a couple of them to flight. I did not intend to say anything during this debate because, like others, I was anxious that it should come to an end. However, upon pressure being brought to bear upon me by some of my maritime colleagues, I yielded against my better judgment. I did not think it was right to allow the Tory member for Queens (Mr. McLure) to have everything to say about conditions in Prince Edward Island. One of my old teachers used to say that when you heard nothing you should say nothing, but here I am afraid I am disobeying him.
I listened attentively but painfully to the doleful speech of the Tory member for Queens. It was a gloomy picture indeed that he gave of conditions in our province. The last part of his speech was brighter, however, because he invited tourists to come down to that terribly neglected province. His speech reminded me of the poet's description of Jacques Cartier's first winter on the St. Lawrence river. He was very gloomy at first because the river was frozen over and there were other conditions which were not very suitable, but later on he changed like my hon. friend. I think the lines of the poet read somewhat as follows:
But when he changed the scene He told how soon it oast In early spring the fetters That held the waters fast.
How the magic wand of summer Cast the landscape of his eyes Like the drybones of the just When they wake in Paradise.
He was referring to the St. Lawrence river and surrounding scenery.

The Address-Mr. Grant
I am sorry the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) is not in his seat at the moment. Before continuing and by way of diversion, may I say that following the last provincial election in my province I understand he gave an interview to the press. I am told that the reason given by him for all C.C.F. candidates having lost their deposits was that the people of Prince Edward Island were not sufficiently educated along C.C.F. lines. I am not finding fault with his way of expressing himself, but I presume he meant that we did not know the C.C.F. party well enough. There is a contradiction here, because the people of Prince Edward Island turned down the Tory party because they knew them too well.
To get back to the Tory member for Queens, his speech was indeed mournful and bewildered. The other day he told the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) that he and the minister had both done well for the province of Prince Edward Island. I think it was ingratitude on his part to ignore the senior member for Queens (Mr. Douglas). I am reminded of the traveller in iEsop's fable who picked up a frozen snake and placed it in his bosom, and after it had warmed up a little it stung him to death. I was surprised to hear such a speech made in this house, especially at a time when the province of Prince Edward Island has never been as prosperous. In fact it looks sometimes as though this is a period of uncontrolled prosperity.
In his speech yesterday the only minister praised by the hon. member was the former minister of fisheries, the late Hon. Mr. Bridges. I suppose he thinks the only good Liberals are dead ones.
The Tory member for Queens deplores the fact that we have not more cold storage plants in Prince Edward Island. His party has been in power in Prince Edward Island, and if he were in his seat tonight I would ask him if he could point to one cold storage plant that the Conservative party ever built in Prince Edward Island. There are in my constituency about five potato warehouses which were built for the benefit of the potato growers and the Liberal party built every one of them. There is one in Souris costing $200,000, another of the same kind in Georgetown, another in Elmira, another in St. Andrews, and another one being built in Morell-all built under a Liberal administration. Not one of those cold storage plants was built by the Conservative party. The Liberals built every one of them. I should like the Tory member for Queens to point out
something that the Conservatives have done in Prince Edward Island, or anywhere else for that matter.
He also spoke about highways. We have a great many highways in Prince Edward Island, hundreds of miles of paved roads running from one end of the province to the other, and the Conservative party did not build one foot of them. They did attempt at one time to build a few miles; but they did not seem to understand how to do it; the frost destroyed the road, and the work had to be all done over again by a succeeding Liberal government.
He also spoke about foxes and reefers. I do not know exactly where his word "reefer" came from, but there is a warm jacket which is known as a reefer and perhaps that is why they call the warm cars reefers. I suggest to my hon. friend that he get one of these reefer coats, if he can get one large enough to button, and then get one of these fox furs and put it around his neck, and then he would not have to do so much talking in the house. We would all know what he stood for-reefers and fox furs.
One strange thing he did say, that all the money that was spent on plants in Prince Edward Island during the war was $1,277. As a matter of fact, there was more money spent in Prince Edward Island for its size than in any other province. Millions of dollars were spent there by the then minister of national defence because he was a member for the province. Millions of dollars were spent on two or three airports. I did not get much in my constituency, but I got elected at the next election. What I did get was an air raid telephone line all along the north shore of my constituency, and after the war was over, the government gave that to the people. It served several parishes. That alone must have cost many thousands of dollars, so that I cannot understand where my hon. friend gets his figure of $1,277.
The Tory member for Queens also complains about our national park and says that the roads leading to it are not good enough. I ask him who built the national park there? What is the national park to any Tory? It was built by the Liberal government, but the Tories can go there, of course. But they never put it there, and they never would put it there. There is one highway to the park. My hon. friend need not complain because his party never did anything like that in our province at least.
Speaking about reefer cars, I should like to put a statement on Hansard with regard to', 'The Address-Mr. Grant
reefer cars in Prince Edward Island. This is taken from the Department of Agriculture in Prince Edward Island:
During the crop season of 1947 there were 8,835 carloads of potatoes ferried across the straits by the Canadian National Railways.
During the same season 858 carloads of turnips were ferried across, making a total of 9,393 cars of potatoes and turnips ferried across the straits.
So the Tory member for Queens had a big job on his hands in arranging for all these cars. Of course he had the assistance of the Minister of Transport, but he had to work pretty hard himself. The minister is a hard worker too,
but I do not think he could ever get along without the aid of his parliamentary assistant, the Tory member tor Queens.
On motion of Mr. Grant the debate was adjourned.']

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) asked a question regarding transportation for wives and dependent members of families of members of parliament over the railways of Canada.
I would reply by saying that members of the House of Commons are entitled by law to free transportation upon all railway trains in Canada. This is by virtue of section 346 of the Railway Act, 1919. Free transportation to dependent members of the families of members of the House of Commons is issued under authority of section 345(c) of the Railway Act.
I am informed by the Canadian National Railways that trip passes issued for their trains to dependent members of the families of members of the House of Commons bear no restriction whatever. The Canadian Pacific Railway, however, advise that trip passes such as I have mentioned are restricted in so far as travel on trains 6 and 15 between Montreal and Toronto is concerned, and trains 355 and 356 between Montreal and Quebec. The company states however that if a member will make known to them at the time a pass is requested that any one of these particular trains is to be used, the restrictions will be removed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should have liked to deliver this speech on health during national health week in Canada, but unfortunately I did not have the opportunity of doing so. During national health week our attention was drawn to the importance of health through articles in the press, ever the radio, by public meetings and by educational programs. Every means was used to direct the attention of the Canadian public to the importance of health, both for the elimination of disease and suffering, and from the standpoint of building a stronger Canadian nation. The House of Commons is one place in particular where this question should be discussed fully. It is not a subject which is commonly debated in the house, except for a few short hours when estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare are under consideration.
Today medical science has made the world healthier than it has ever been. But what has been accomplished in scientific medicine is small when we consider the future possibilities of preventing disease, alleviating suffering and prolonging human life. The best definition of an ideal situation regarding health is found in the constitution of the world health organization, which states:
Enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of health is one of the fundamental rights of every human being, without distinction as to race, political belief, economic or social conditions.
We in Canada might well regard this as our objective so far as the health of the Canadian people is concerned. At different times in the House of Commons I have quoted statistics and placed on record figures to show that we have been lax in dealing with a problem of such marked importance to our people. There has been little change in the statistics, although there are some encouraging features. There has been a drop in the maternal and infantile mortality rate, but still more work can be done in these and other fields of national
5849-113J
The Address-Mr. Blair

health. While educational programs have shown rich benefits, we are still faced with the problem of opportunity to receive necessary treatment.
A year ago I drew the attention of the house to the high cost of hospitalization and treatment. I pointed out at that time that the costs were becoming so high that the average citizen could not afford to pay for hospital treatment. This condition has not improved; and with the rising cost of living it has become much worse. We are still faced with the high cost of hospital construction, the maintenance of existing hospitals, and the shortage of nursing staff. Statistics in the various provinces differ. We must realize in investigating these statistics that the health of a Canadian citizen in any one province is as much a matter of importance to the Canadian nation as the health of a Canadian in any other province.
Even if we have made advances in the matter of infantile mortality, there is no reason to feel complacent. Our infant mortality rate for the year 1945, the last year for which I have the figures, stands at 51 per thousand live births. The rate in the United States is 38. In fact New Zealand, Australia, Sweden, Iceland, The Netherlands, Norway, South Africa, England and Denmark all have lower infantile mortality rates than we have. I draw attention to the difference in the infantile mortality rate in the United States and in Canada, that is, the United States with 38 and Canada with 51 per 1,000 live births. This is something difficult to comprehend in view of the fact that the United States has such large cities and urban centres. In 1945, when the dominion rate was 51, the provinces had the following rates:
Ontario	 41
British Columbia	 42
Alberta	 43
Saskatchewan	 44
Prince Edward Island	 45
Manitoba	 48
Nova Scotia	 53
Quebec	 62
New Brunswick	 71
In 1945 we lost 14,823 infants, a large percentage of whom could have been saved by adequate treatment and care. The matter of an immigration policy absorbs much of the time of this house, but in losing those 15,000 children we lost the finest type of little immigrants that could come into this country. They were children of French, English, Irish and Scotch parentage, they were the children of those other hardy races which came to Canada and helped to build up this country. While such conditions exist the saving of such little citizens should receive priority in parlia-
mentary discussion over debates on immigration. An immigration policy is necessary but such a policy is unsound when we are forced to replace 15,000 little Canadian citizens with people brought in from other lands. I am not averse to an immigration policy and the bringing in of citizens from other lands, but I feel that in carrying out such a policy we should also pay attention to the 15,000 little immigrants who came into this country in that year.
The number of infants dying from communicable diseases in 1945 stood at about the same rate as in former years. In that year the number of deaths was 1,040. A large number of those small children could have been saved by immunization. If preventive measures had been taken we could have saved many of them, but the difficulty is that preventive measures are not equally available in all parts of Canada. At the beginning of my speech I referred to the shortage of hospital facilities. We have generally believed in Canada that 4-5 beds per hundred of population was sufficient for our needs, but the number of hospital beds throughout the province varies from three per hundred in Prince Pldward Island to seven and eight per hundred in Alberta and British Columbia. Even in those provinces with the greatest number of beds there are many hospitals with long waiting lists.
The costs of hospitalization have increased tremendously but the value of the services given in hospital has also increased tremendously. The average stay in hospital has dropped from about twenty days to around nine days per patient. However, it is a fact that today many people are faced with costs which are difficult to meet, especially by people in the lower income tax brackets. It is unfortunate that in a country with a scattered population we cannot go as far as is necessary to meet the needs of the people. Costs are high not only in existing hospitals but in those areas where extra accommodation is required. Construction costs have reached an almost prohibitive figure.
Under present conditions the cost of providing new hospital accommodation is around $8,000 to $9,000 per bed. At that rate the construction of a fifty-bed hospital will cost almost half a million dollars, which is a heavy debt for many small municipalities or towns to assume. According to a return made by !he Department of National Health and Welfare, as of June. 1947, we still required 5,000 beds for tubercular patients. It is impossible to eliminate tuberculosis or put on an all-out program for the prevention and cure of tuber-

The Address-Mr. Blair
culosis as long as such shortages exist. It is admitted that there is an increased demand for hospitalization and that the demand for hospitalization far exceeds the supply at the present time. This causes considerable hardship, and it means that there is a lack of proper care. Because of the shortage of nurses, which totals approximately 10,000, the staffing of new or existing hospitals is very difficult.
Many hospital boards have planned new building projects or extensions but the cost is entirely beyond their financial means. In order properly to take care of sickness in this dominion the distribution of Canadian doctors from province to province and from urban to rural areas must be considered. Most urban districts have an adequate supply of doctors, but according to a return from the Department of National Health and Welfare, the following ratio of doctors to population exists:

It is estimated that at the end of 1947 there were in Canada 13,419 active physicians, which with an estimated population of 12,300,000 gives us one physician for every 916 of population. This situation is not as bad as it first appears. Urban areas have a concentration of hospitals and specialists and the statistics show that from twenty to fifty per cent of the patients are from rural areas. We should take steps to make the conditions and financial awards of those doctors practising in out-oftown areas more satisfactory in order that the younger group of doctors starting to practise may be induced to settle in rural districts.
It is not my intention to present to parliament health statistics which I have given in previous years. The conditions have not varied greatly and the percentages are practically the same. Some action has been taken in the matter of cancer research by the Department of National Health and Welfare. This is a
step in the right direction, in view of the annual death rate in Canada of over 14,000 citizens from this terrible disease. Research should be given all possible encouragement and treatment facilities so broadened that all citizens may have the opportunity for early diagnosis and treatment.
I am not impressed by the so-called total war on arthritis, as announced by the department. During the last session of parliament when the matter of arthritis came up in the course of a debate on health estimates, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) stated that a conference of government and professional authorities would be called-I quote the minister's own words- "to see if we cannot provide some co-ordinating authority to carry on in the field of arthritis". We must remember that there are some 600,000 sufferers from this disease, of whom 125,000 are crippled, either bed or wheel-chair patients, without any hope of gainful employment. Many have spent all their available funds in hospitalization or on long and expensive treatment. Rheumatic disease is the cause of one-sixth of all industrial invalidism. Since up to the present there is no specific cure, it has been viewed in a spirit of hopelessness. It has been misunderstood, described by many medical terms, and is often confused with rheumatic fever. There is a tendency to group all the diseases of this nature under the common term "rheumatism". Rheumatic fever is most frequent in the young from five to fifteen years of age and often leaves a damaged heart. Many of the most destructive forms of arthritis cripple the patient between the ages of twenty and forty, which is the period of greatest productivity. Millions of dollars have been spent annually by sufferers from rheumatism. It is obvious that, since there is no single method of treatment, there is no specific cure. Every effort should be made to save these patients from crippling, apart from the relief of pain and suffering. We should not consider them hopeless.
The result of the conference on arthritis in Ottawa last November was a decision to carry out the program of arthritis in the Department of Veterans Affairs hospital at Sunnybrook. Arthritis exists from coast to coast; we find these unfortunate patients in the wards and rooms of all our public hospitals. It may be possible to do research at Sunnybrook, but D.V.A. hospitals could not possibly accommodate all the arthritis patients seeking admission. There is no provision, even in Sunnybrook, for female patients. The only women patients obtaining entrance at Sunnybrook are a few army nurses who were unfortunate enough to develop this disease. I
The Address-Mr. Blair

question the ability of the Department of Veterans Affairs to handle the situation. They have not on the staffs of their hospitals sufficient physicians and personnel trained in arthritis to carry out such a program effectively. There is a marked shortage of physicians trained1 in arthritis clinics. Even if the D.V.A. undertakes to train men in the treatment of arthritis, these men will later on, when they go out to run their own offices, have no access to such equipment-and some of it is very expensive-or to facilities for treatment. There are in the dominion many general hospitals and many good physicians. Under present conditions with the D.V.A. arthritis clinic located in Sunnybrook, these men are shut off from all help and assistance. Every general hospital and every physician has a percentage of arthritis patients. I speak from my own knowledge. It is a problem for all general hospitals in Canada. The patients are there demanding treatment, and the doctors and the staff of these hospitals, and the general practitioners throughout Canada, should be given help. We must not forget that we have 125,000 invalids or semi-invalids among 600,000 arthritis sufferers. While I admit the necessity of research, yet I suggest action and help for all arthritis sufferers. Even if we have not yet a specific cure, many of these cases could be saved from crippling disabilities by adequate treatment.
I have criticized this set-up of the Department of National Health and Welfare at Sunnybrook, and having criticized it, I feel that I should offer some constructive suggestions for dealing with this question.
1.	There should be increased facilities for treatment in the hospitals throughout the country.
2.	There should be sufficient beds for these patients; physiotherapy, equipment and trained personnel.
3.	There should be institutions for the special care of arthritis patients where they can receive specialized diagnosis and treatment.
4.	Medical colleges should teach the care of arthritis to students and internes so that when they go out in practice they have a working knowledge of the subject and the basic principles of diagnosis and treatment.
5.	Medical schools and teaching hospitals could be made the basis of arthritic centres instead1 of limiting the efforts to the D.V.A.
6.	There are no places in Canada where men can be trained for this specialty and therefore grants should be given to universities to train suitable men for teaching purposes. This could take the form of travelling fellowships for professional men who desire to take training.

In the consideration of matters affecting national health, proper and adequate nutrition is of marked importance. This applies particularly to veterans suffering disabilities from war services, and those veterans who by reason of their age receive the veterans' allowances. War veterans' pensions and allowances must be increased to the poiifc, having regard to the high cost of living, vwhere the veterans can maintain a decent standard of living. Old age pensions under present conditions are not sufficient to maintain a standard of life of which we can feel proud. There are many, and I have particularly noted this fact, especially in the age group 67, 68 and 69, who, by reason of physical disabilities and age, are deserving of allowances but under present legislation are not eligible.
Speaking on the matter of health, I wish to direct the attention of the house to certain regulations made by the Department of Transport, radio communications division. These are regulations governing wave lengths for electrotherapeutie equipment for use by the medical profession. This is a type of treatment which has come into common use in Canada and the United States and which gives beneficial results.
In December, 1946. a new wave length was set at 10-98 metres for medical diathermy machines. A few manufacturers sent in machines for tests, both in Washington and in Ottawa, and received approval of this wave length. Under a new regulation passed on October 27, 1947, however, another set of rules was given by the radio division of the Department of Transport which changed the wave length from 10-98 to 11-06 metres. Manufacturers making these machines, and physicians purchasing them, have had to change the type of machines used.
The Canadian Medical Association and the Canadian Hospital Council both made protests to the government over the short time limit allowed in Canada, that is, until January 1, 1948. It is true there was considerable notice given of these requirements at the time, but hospitals have found it difficult to obtain the equipment which they would like, and that which is available is in short supply.
The federal communications commission of the United States allows five years, from July 1, 1948, for users of these machines to conform to the new regulations, but in Canada the users of these machines were simply cut off on January 1, 1948. The United States allows five years in which these machines can be replaced. The regulations axe supposed to be international, yet doctors or hospitals in cities close to our border, for instance in

The Address-Mr. Blair
Plattsburg, may continue to use old machines while in Montreal they may not, and naturally a machine just across the line would interfere just as much as one in Canada.
I would like to read and place on the record a resolution passed by the Canadian Hospital Council in October, 1947.
At the Winnipeg meeting, the Canadian Hospital Council passed the following resolution unanimously:
Whereas the recent announcement by the Department of Transport that all eleetrothera-peutic equipment emanating interference must be either completely screened or replaced by equipment so constructed that it w'ill disseminate waves on three designated wave lengths alone; and
Whereas it will be exceedingly difficult for the hospitals to comply with this regulation in the time stipulated, partly because of the difficulty of obtaining adequate screening or ia sufficient number of properly constructed new type machines and also because of the marked expense involved; and	_
Whereas, under similar conditions, the United States government permits the hospitals a period of five years within which to replace the present machines, and interference from machines in the United States will affect Canadian reception during that period;
Be it resolved that the Canadian Hospital Council respectfully request the Canadian government to so modify the regulations respecting radio interference by elecitrotherapeutie equipment that the use of old equipment be permissible for a period of another five years but that all new equipment purchased during that period be of the new crystal controlled type.
If Canadian hospitals have to replace this equipment with new machinery, or if they have to go to the trouble and expense of screening this equipment, it will involve a good deal of money, and hospitals at the present time are having their own difficulties financing their own institutions, without submitting to a rule of this type.
The Canadian radio department is not equipped to find out whether certain machines do interfere. They have one testing equipment in Canada, and that is in Ottawa. This is an important matter because there are about 10.000 diathermy machines in Canada. Time should be given to permit manufacturers to try to develop some means of converting the old machines now in use to the new wave length and thus save hospitals and doctors thousands of dollars.
Under present conditions a physician or a hospital using a machine since January 1, 1948, must either purchase a new machine with the new wave length or go to the great expense of shielding by a lead-lined room. The use of screened treatment rooms in hospitals is cheaper, but it prevents the taking of these machines to the rooms and to the hospital wards, and even if doctors and hospitals can
afford the investment of replacing old machines with new ones built to the new specifications of wave length, it will probably be two or three years before sufficient machines can be manufactured to meet the demand.
The departments state that they do not contemplate extending the above date for suppression of excessive radiation. It is of peculiar interest to note that while radio communications for ships at war, aeroplanes and radar are now considered important in peacetime, there was no move during the war to stop the use of these machines when our communications were vital. The regulations are supposed to be international, but the United States has given a five-year extension. In view of this there is no reason why radio experts or the technicians of the radio department-of Canada should use such arbitrary measures in dealing with a matter where such equipment is used for the purpose of treatment by Canadian doctors and Canadian hospitals.
In the early part of this speech I dealt with certain conditions regarding lack of hospital facilities, shortage of nurses, and opportunity for treatment. I pointed out the glaring need for action as regards our heavy infantile mortality. In previous speeches I have called the attention of the house to the need for early action to correct these deficiencies in health matters in Canada.
As each province has control of legislation affecting health matters, it is very apparent that the provinces must receive assistance in order that a common plan for the benefit of all Canada may be produced. Provinces have different standards of health and varying facilities. There have been reports from Ottawa of a national health insurance scheme. The government has taken the position, if one may judge from some of their speakers, that owing to the absence of financial agreement between the Drew government in Ontario and the Duplessis government in Quebec, action is prevented. The premiers of these two provinces have both on several occasions in public strongly urged, and intimated their willingness to participate in further discussion of these matters in a dominion-provincial conference. There is no doubt that there is a certain amount of stubbornness in the government at Ottawa which prevents a resumption of the conference. To me this is something difficult to comprehend. The saving of life and the relief of human suffering should receive consideration above any political bickering.
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Tucker) made a speech in Toronto early in February in which he intimated that Ottawa is not prepared to
-rter

The Address-Mr. Blair
go ahead with health insurance. I wish to quote from the Toronto Star of February 4. Incidentally, this was headed, "No health insurance, Tucker from the prairies says." I quote:
*Speaking before the Liberal businessmen's club of Toronto, he said that administration of the scheme would be left to the provinces, which would pay 20 per cent. The balance of 20 per cent would be split evenly between the municipalities and the individuals participating.
Incidentally I notice this is another time when people seem to make very important announcements outside parliament. It was amazing to read this in the Star. Continuing:
"Cost would be about $30 per person per year, of which the individual would contribute about $3," Mr. Tucker said.
Possibly this too is news to the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

speechtext:
To continue the quotation:
It would include all present health services as well as all branches of medical, surgical, nursing, dental, hospital, pharmaceutical and optometrical services. The individual would have a free choice of doctor and hospital. Outlying areas would be served by travelling clinics.
He intimated that the failure to proceed with a health program-and we have it again -was due to the absence of a financial agreement between the dominion and the provinces. I think I read a speech made by the minister in Quebec, and he mentioned something about a red herring. Possibly he felt that, being near the maritime districts, he should say something about fisheries too. I hope this portfolio is not saddled on him.
The member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), in an amazing statement, is reported as saying that the dominion is prepared to pay sixty per cent of the cost of the health insurance scheme. Under this the provinces would pay twenty per cent and the remaining twenty per cent would be split between the municipality and the individual. The cost would be about $30 per person annually and the individual would contribute only S3. This looks like an entirely new scheme if the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs has been quoted correctly; or it may be possible that he has been talking about something without knowledge of the subject. In order to achieve the desired result from the standpoint of the Canadian nation, nothing can be done, nor can a proper plan be brought into existence, without an agreement and the consent of all the provinces in matters of taxation. It is obvious that any

other proposal would be only a partial plan, or a failure, in so far as all Canada is concerned.
The time has come, Mr. Speaker, to enunciate and put into effect a national health program for Canada. We have fallen far short of the objective of the world health organization. The objective plan of this party is one which will bring physical and mental health to every Canadian citizen, regardless of race, economic status or geographical position. There are certain basic features necessary at present to any plan and without which a plan cannot succeed. In our judgment grants should be given for hospital construction and expansion. Existing health insurance plans should be investigated with a view to their possible amalgamation, and enlarged as the basis for a contributory health insurance plan which should be inaugurated. That is, we would take the best features out of all the plans. This would make health services available to all at a minimum of expense. We believe that there must be a free choice between doctor and patient, and that in order for the plan to be successful it must be brought into effect with the full co-operation of dominion, provincial and municipal governments, and the medical association. I mention the medical association because in any plan that is adopted, the doctors must not become civil servants. With this full co-operation, there is every reason to believe that this will be the solution to the problems which I have mentioned today. Sickness is costing the people of Canada a billion dollars a year in loss of production, absence from work, and cost of illness. A health insurance plan will be expensive, but above all it will pay dividends in the relief of human suffering. This is not a time for political bickering and inaction. The health of the citizens of Canada should be the paramount consideration.
Medical science has today reached a high standard. It has opened up new fields of treatment in the prevention of disease which were unknown a few years ago. We must take full advantage of all that science offers for the relief of human suffering. The health of the people of Canada should be a matter for the federal government to consider far above many of the affairs which now engage the attention of parliament. In six years of war we lost 45.000 men. who were either killed in battle or died of disease; but in the years following the war we still lose thousands of Canadian people whose death could have been prevented. We were successful in the battle against our enemies in the war in the cause of freedom. We should continue the battle

The Address-Mr. J. H. Matthews
against disease which is causing such tremendous casualties among our people. We should fight not only for better facilities for treatment and cure of disease, but also for those other things upon which health is dependent- elimination of slums, facilfties of education, and adequate nutrition. We must realize that the raising of the standard of living is an important factor in the national problem of health. We must realize above all that little in this life is of importance without health.

speechtext:
In rising to participate in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I want to bring one or two matters to the attention of the house.
First of all I want to refer briefly to a bill which was passed in this house during the 1917 session of parliament. It was a bill designed to repeal the Chinese Immigration Act. I remember, sir, that there was a prolonged and very interesting debate at that time and many divergent views were expressed, partly because of a lack of a definite government policy in regard to people of the Chinese race. The leader of this C.C.F. group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) at that time expressed his keen disappointment in the bill because it failed to carry out the promise made by the Prime Minister, who had given out a press statement saying that "the effect of the repeal will be to remove all discrimination against the Chinese on account of race and to bring Chinese persons under the general provisions of the Immigration Act, and no longer under legislation applying exclusively to persons of Chinese origin."
The bill which we passed, sir, did not remove all discrimination against people of the Chinese race. It did permit, however, the entry of the wife and children of Chinese residents in Canada who had become Canadian citizens; but the discrimination was continued against those who had not become Canadian citizens. I have in my hand at this moment a clipping from the columns of the Ottawa Journal, dated Monday, February 16, which is headed with these significant words:	"No Chinese
wives have entered Canada since ban lifted." It reads as follows:
Resources Minister Glen was told today that not a single wife or child of a Chinese-Canadian citizen has entered Canada since it became legally possible nearly a year ago.
.An eight-man delegation from the committee for the repeal of the Chinese Immigration Act made that statement to Mr. Glen, Minister of Immigration, while urging repeal of an order in council which prevents wives and children in China from joining Chinese here who are not Canadian citizens. Repeal of the Chinese Immigration Act about a year ago technically allowed in the families of those who had become citizens.
In answer to their charge that the change had so far meant nothing, Mr. Glen said the department was only getting to the point where administrative difficulties could be cleared up and an immigration officer appointed to go to Hong Kong. The officer had only been chosen this week.
However, it would probably be some time before there was any movement of families because an office would have to be found in Hong Kong and there would be other problems.
At a press conference following what he described as "<a sympathetic hearing," Irving Himel, of Toronto, legal counsel, estimated that something fewer than one hundred applications for family movements must be on file with the government.
The delegation criticized the continuing prohibition against families of non-citizens as unnatural and morally wrong and in contradiction of a stand Canada had taken in united nations councils in arguing that husbands and wives should be allowed bo live together as a matter of principle.	[DOT]
Reverend Doctor A. E. Armstrong, of Toronto, head of the Canadian council of churches, said the Protestant churches were against the government han. It was estimated by the delegation that repeal of the order in council would mean the coming to Canada of between three thousand and four thousand Chinese during a ten-year period.
It would appear that the members of this delegation feel that things have been moving altogether too slowly as far as the admission of Chinese wives and children to Canada is concerned. I can quite understand how difficult it is for a department to act rapidly and function properly in a world as dislocated as our world is today, but I too would express the hope that every effort might now be put forth to facilitate the reunion of these long-separated families. But this is not my only appeal. In the lifting of the ban against the admission of wives and children of Canadian citizens of Chinese origin, Canada took a definite step forward, but only a step. She could have gone and I believe should have gone further. On the highest of moral and spiritual grounds we should have permitted the entrance of the wives and children of all Chinese now resident in Canada, whether or not they have become Canadian citizens. In fact I believe such a step would go far toward leading more of our Chinese residents to seek to become citizens of Canada. The fact that the Protestant churches of Canada are against the perpetuation of this ban is significant indeed, and I believe should carry considerable weight with the government. I believe, too, that the strength and soul of the Roman Catholic church also support this appeal. As I understand it the Roman Catholic church has always taken a very strong stand on the question of divorce, holding inviolate the sanctity of marriage. Yet there are Chinese

scattered across all the provinces of this dominion who have not seen their wives and children for many years. We hold up our hands in horror and disgust when we learn that in spite of our diplomatic representations Russia refuses to allow her womenfolk to leave that country and join their Canadian husbands. As a nation Canada has taken a strong stand in regard to these matters in the united nations assembly; yet our actions here at home are a direct negation of the very high principles we profess.
In making this appeal to the government today I want to make it quite clear that I am not advocating the unrestricted immigration of all classes of Chinese into Canada. I only ask for the admission of the wives and children of Chinese who are now resident in Canada, because I do feel that we have no moral right to keep families apart, as we have done in the past. The second matter I want to deal with at this time has to do with the work of radiotelegraph operators on the British Columbia coast. To introduce this matter I should like to read another short clipping, this time culled from the columns of the C.C.F. News of Thursday, February 19, and coming from Vancouver, British Columbia:
Union shows need for radio operators on coastal ships
Discontinuance of protection afforded the travelling public and ships' crews, through elimination of full-time radiotelegraph operators, is forecast by a recommendation of the new maritime commission.
Division 59 of the commercial telegraphers' union (AFL), whose members include most of the radio operators carried on B.C. coastal passenger vessels, has been pressing Ottawa fo-r stricter regulations to insure proper radio service on these ships. In the latest brief submitted it. is pointed out that some ships have never maintained an efficient radio department while on many it has been voluntary and limited to a radiophone with no certified operator.
The Canada 'Shipping Act governing these conditions is so full of loopholes, according to a union spokesman, that it is actually permissible for a ship of any size and capacity to operate anywhere on the B.C. coast entirely without radio, by merely arranging her schedule suitably. A number of B.C. coast ships do just that, while others flout this archaic law by carrying one man in a combined position of purser-operator or freight clerk-operator, in which radio duties are side-tracked. Less than a dozen B.C. coast ships maintain a proper radio service, it is reported.

The CTU's protests against this disgraceful situation have been repeatedly turned down by Ottawa for several years, and when it recently put in specific requests for amending the act to eliminate these evils the Minister of Transport replied "The (maritime commission) does not believe that coastal vessels should be compelled to have a full-time radio operator, but it thinks that the duties of the radio operator should be combined with those of one of the mates or purser or freight clerks."
The brief submitted by the local operators pointed out the thousands of lives and huge value of property that has been saved from loss at sea over some thirty-five years by the availability of radio communications; it also showed some of the shortcomings of radiophones and pointed out the vital need of having certified operators giving full time to the radio service.
It reminded the department that on the B.C. coast this service costs the ship but $11 a day, and some of these ships carry over 1,900 persons. But Ottawa apparently does not consider the safety of 1.000 persons and a ship worth up to several million dollars justifies demanding an $ll-a-day service.
Discontinuance of full-time operators would also result in the laying-off of the present experienced staff, most of whom have given over a quarter of a century of excellent service. Many of them are veterans of one war at sea, some of two. Curtailment of radiotelegraph service on B.C. coast vessels has already hit two of these men, while further reductions appear imminent.
As one who in years past has travelled considerably up and down the Pacific coast of British Columbia, I feel disturbed by this move to eliminate gradually the radio operators from our coastal vessels. This move may not greatly disturb people in the inland areas of Canada, but those whose duties take them down to the sea in ships certainly cannot view this trend with any degree of complacency.
The oceans that lap our shores have given to us far too many tragic marine disasters, with their appalling loss of life and property; and the development of radio, and the presence of radio equipment on board, serviced by experienced operators, has done much to allay the fears of the travelling public. I believe we should be extremely careful just now lest in the interest of so-called economy we destroy the very protection we have so consistently built up.
Our maritime commission is a newly established body. They have still to prove themselves before the Canadian public. It would be regrettable indeed if their earlier recommendations should produce such a disastrous effect. Radio contacts, whether on land or sea or in the air, are priceless in times of emergency and need.
The suggestion, then, that the duties of radio operator should be combined with those of one of the mates, or the purser, or the freight clerk, is simply not good enough. A

The Address-Mr. J. L. Gibson
sea tragedy may occur, and the S.O.S. signal might go unheard while other required duties were being performed by the radio operator. Therefore I have no hesitation in telling parliament that this is not economy at all. It is sheer madness, and I am absolutely opposed to it. I would go further and demand that instead of dispensing with the full-time service of radio operators, all vessels should be equipped with radar facilities, and that the shipping laws should be amended to require each vessel to carry as part of its personnel a man who is able not only to operate these devices, but also to repair them when necessary.
What is $11 a day in comparison with the safety of a ship and the lives of all on board? I leave it to hon. members to answer this for themselves. I can well imagine the outcry that would be heard if it were suggested that radio operators should be removed from our air lines. I know every effort has been put forth in the past to make Canadians air-minded. Our Trans-Canada Air Lines and Canadian Pacific Air Lines have built up for themselves a most enviable reputation for safety, security and service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne has covered a 5849-1141
wide range of subjects, some of which I should think might better be discussed when departmental estimates are before the committee. However, there are two or three matters which to my mind are urgent and which I should like now to bring to the attention of the house.
The first subject which comes to mind, and which I think requires some discussion, is that of veterans' pensions. I entertain the fond hope that before the government brings in its final bill covering veterans' pensions it will reconsider its most recent and, may I say, its most generous decision to date; it is not actually generous, but certainly it is more generous than the announcement made on December 19, which to my mind was a shabby statement. The recent announcement was somewhat better; still I do not think it is adequate to meet the need it is supposed to cover.
I have heard many excellent speeches from all sides of the house. Perhaps I should not mention any in particular, but I can say that I received a great deal of information from the speeches of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) made an excellent speech on the subject. I do not confine my comments to members of the Progressive Conservative party, although those are the names which come first to my mind. I think it is unfortunate that on so many occasions in the house we should witness the spectacle of gallant soldiers urging better treatment of their comrades. I believe all hon. members are interested in doing the right thing for those who did so much for us in both world wars.
Today I thought I should like to express in some measure the views of the average civilian in Canada who did not have the opportunity or privilege of wearing the king's uniform in either war. I believe that the civilians of Canada have done particularly well. It may be a strange thing to say, but it seems to me that, as a result of world war I and world war II, our standard of living has advanced measurably. I do not think the same thing can be said of the conditions faced by our veterans, particularly those who suffered disabilities through fighting for us.
I often feel a sense of shame-I am sure many other civilians have the same experience -when I associate with veterans in the legion and other organizations, particularly with pensioners; I have a feeling that we have not done as much as we should have done. I think it must be admitted that civilians in Canada have better homes and better jobs. Many
The Address-Mr. J. L. Gibson

companies have started insurance and pension schemes for their employees. Our standards of education have advanced. The government has done its utmost to see that no undue profits were made out of the war; but, despite that, many companies have been able to extend their plants and build up financial reserves. There are also refundable taxes which will be coming back to them in due course.
Since 1925 there has been an increase of approximately 16 per cent in pensions, but actually this represents a decrease in purchasing power. We must face up to the fact that with the present rates of pension the disabled pensioner is forced to live in mean surroundings. The wife or widow of the pensioner must dress more shabbily than the average woman in our population. It means that most of their children receive an education inferior to that received by other children.
I do not believe that is the desire of civilians in Canada. I do not think that is all we want to do for these people who have done so much for us. At the same time I think most people fee! that the veterans of world war II who were not disabled have had a good deal. The government of the day has done an excellent job in re-establishing them in civilian life. I think every Canadian is glad to have participated in the putting up of the billion and a half dollars or so which we have invested in the rehabilitation of our veterans.
It is difficult for me to understand the niggardliness of the government in the present instance. On December 19 the announcement was made of an increase of $7,500,000 in veterans' pensions, but that was lumped in with the announcement of an increase of $17,500,000 in the pay of civil servants. In fairness to the veterans I think the increase in pensions warranted a separate statement. The Canadian people do not want to be misled and I do not think the government has any intention of trying to mislead them, but at the same time I think we should have had a separate statement.
As announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) recently, the pensions were increased by 16 per cent. The legion suggested an increase of 25 per cent as being fair and I think they were most reasonable in their request. I certainly appreciate the way in which the cabinet guards our money. It would be easy to accede to every demand for more of this and more of that, particularly when it might be a sound political move. I am certainly finding no fault with the way

in which the cabinet guards the taxpayers' money, but in this particular instance I think the cabinet has been too careful. I think the members of the cabinet should meet the wishes of the average Canadian citizen.
Those who stayed at home were able to earn big wages or make reasonably largo profits. As their contribution they were asked to invest in victory bonds. We have said to them, "We will pay you $400,000,000 a year as interest on the money you have lent to prosecute the war." We have also said, "Any time you want to renege you can go into the market place and for every $100 you lent you can get $102, or even S106 in some instances." Those people who lent money' to the government during the war are infinitely better off than those who went overseas to fight for us. Those veterans who sacrificed everything they' had, had no opportunity of participating in war profits. Some of them suffered permanent impairment of health and many of their widows must face tragically blasted lives. But we say to those people, "We cannot afford to pay' you one-quarter as much as we pay each y'ear to the people who lent money."
By paying out another $10,000,000 the country could meet the wishes of the Canadian Legion. We could do the right thing. I am sure there is not an hon. member who would not gladly' vote that money. I am sure there is not a taxpayer in Canada who would not be happy and honoured to pay that money. I want to make an appeal to the cabinet. They are all businessmen, and it is hard for me to understand why they are not ready to protect the investment that has been made in our veterans.

I should like to say a few words to the Prime Minister who unfortunately is not in his seat at the moment. He rarely calls mo in to consult with him, but I should like to bring to his attention the fact that British Columbia has no cabinet minister. In bringing up this matter I want to assure the house that I am not talking for myself. I am quite certain that hon. members in all corners of the house regret the passing to another place of our good friend, the former Minister of Veterans Affairs, the Right Hon. Ian A. Mackenzie. He was a good friend to all of us, and I know the veterans of Canada will long remember the advanced legislation on their behalf which he presented to this house. I myself wish him long life and many happy hours in his new abode in the senate. I want to say to that gallant soldier who replaces him as Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) that I am sure he will make a great contribution to the welfare of his comrades in the direction of the department of which he is how the head.
It appears to me, Mr. Speaker, that it is about time that the folks back here in eastern Canada realized that British Columbia is getting to be a great big country. We have always had a vast area out there but have been short on population. Today we have over one million people in that province, and the highest per capita income of any people in Canada. The people of British Columbia are the highest taxpayers per capita in the whole dominion. British Columbia has also been extremely co-operative with the dominion. It took the lead in the dominion-provincial conference, and if there is any political pay-off British Columbia ought to do at least as well in cabinet representation as Ontario and Quebec. Quebec with its 3,000,000 people is favoured with six cabinet ministers in addition to the distinguished member who occupies the Speaker's chair. It seems to me that it is time that British Columbia was recognized for its stature and its worth by the appointment of two cabinet ministers.

I come now to a matter that is of grave concern to business, large and small, in Canada. I come here from the constituency of Comox-AIberni, which is the great home of free enterprise in Canada. We have businesses there both very large and very small, and many in between. I think of the small loggers in my riding, owning probably only an axe, a saw and a pump jack. I think of the fishermen with their small boats, each of whom is a private enterpriser owning his own business and taking orders from no one. He wears no man's collar, not even a socialist collar. I think, too, of very large industries in my riding which have been most successful.
What concerns me is the apparent indifference of this free-enterprise government-I was going to say this so-called free-enterprise government, and I think that is better-to attacks on successful businessmen by irresponsible members of the house. I have been surprised that no minister felt called upon to defend from such attacks successful businessmen who are paying such a large proportion of the taxes which go into the public treasury and are doing all that free enterprise can do. I do not think ill-considered, derogatory remarks against successful businessmen,.

coming particularly from my C.C.F. friends opposite, should be allowed to go unchallenged in this house. I do not consider it the duty of private members of the house to be rising in their places all the time and challenging these statements. I find the government unwilling to defend that type of enterprise, and I do not think that is good enough. I trust that the members of the cabinet will take this matter into their consideration and see whether something cannot be done about it, because I am tired of having to take care of the C.C.F. myself.

I should like to give my own rough analysis of the operations of this gang, so called by the C.C.F., and see if anything in their fair province of Saskatchewan can show anything like a similar record. Last year, by this company's operations in the markets of the world, the dominion government received $7,682,000, for which the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) is very grateful. From Saskatchewan government enterprise he did not get anything. The employees who work for Mr. MacMillan and his corporation received double the Saskatchewan rate of wages, and on top of that they also received $1,382,000 in the form of cash bonuses and in funds set aside to care for their pensions. The shareholders at the same time received a cash dividend of $782,000, or 1-5 cents on each dollar's worth of business done. That left in the company's treasury approximately $6,000,000. And here is where socialist thinking goes off the rails. In the
