speechtext:
My intention in taking part in this debate at this stage, Mr. Speaker, is not to delay unduly the proceedings of this house by making extended remarks but rather to emphasize some of the points which undoubtedly some of the other speakers have already touched upon, but which I feel should, be reiterated in view of the recent turn of world affairs.

I have the honour to represent Compton county in this honourable house, which county forms one of the eleven ridings known as the eastern townships in the province of Quebec. Its main occupations are agriculture, industrial occupations and lumbering. Its people consist of descendants of loyalist stock and early French settlers; and in this section of the countiy we find no problem of Canadian unity, being all proud as we are of the name of Canadians, believing Canada to be the best country to live in today, and therefore believing heartily in the summing up contained in an article in the Atlantic magazine of January last, which states:
The various pieces of very complex national policy which Canada is fashioning fit together into a long-range program which shows solid and consistent thought, and1 is a credit to what is perhaps the best managed democracy on earth.
This declaration, coming as it does from a neutral and outside source surveying and commenting upon world affairs, as it has done for the past ninety years, is high tribute to our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and also to the members of his cabinet. There is perhaps an additional reason for pride and appreciation on the part of the eastern townships with regard to this declaration, since we have a native son of Compton among the cabinet ministers in the person of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), whose Canadianism and statesmanship have brought pride and admiration not only to Compton county, not only to the eastern townships, but to the whole country at large.
Since the close of the war the attention of the world has been focused on the possibilities of European recovery. The trade agreements signed at Geneva, the ITO conference at Havana, the restriction of Canadian imports and consumption, the recalling of the United States congress at an earlier day than usual, and likewise the calling of our own parliament in December last-all these events serve to underline the obvious fact that all parts of the world suffer when great trading areas are disabled. Satisfactory trade relations for any country can develop only as rehabilitation of such trading areas proceeds.
As is well known, Canada is in an outstanding position as a world trader, and the recent Geneva trade agreement is of the utmost importance to the people of Canada and its economy. That Canada has a great economic interest in Europe's recovery cannot be denied. It may not always be realized that, before the war, western Europe-now representing those European countries outside the Russian sphere-and the United Kingdom

The Address-Mr. Blanchette
together accounted for almost forty-five per cent of the total world trade. Since the war, forty per cent of Canadian exports went to Britain and western Europe during the first nine months of 1947. The importance for Canada of European developments is revealed especially when these exports are broken down into groups of commodities. Britain and western Europe were taking all our exported wheat and nearly two-thirds of our flour. Britain is the principal market for our meat, cheese and eggs. It also takes a third of our exports of planks and boards and all our pit props. Western Europe and Britain absorb a third of our nickel, half of our zinc and lead, two-thirds of our aluminum and four-fifths of our copper. Western Europe is taking two-thirds of our rubber products, most of our locomotives and the greater part of our ships. It is therefore apparent that the prosperity of all the regions of Canada, from the maritimes to British Columbia, is dependent to a certain extent on what happens in Europe.
The Geneva trade agreements entered into by twenty-three separate countries are for three years' duration, so that at the end of that time Canada shall be free either to continue or to refuse to renew these agreements. Our 1935 trade agreement with the United States was for three years and this has continued since with no disturbance. In addition, the Geneva trade agreements prepared a draft charter for a world trade organization. I sincerely feel that it is to the interest of Canada, of labour and agriculture, to accept these trade agreements in order that the country may continue to progress and to obtain its large share of the world export trade.
A recent release supplies the information that under the Marshall plan, which is to be accepted shortly by the United States congress-let us all hope-Canada is to share the greater portion of the $2 billion total which will be provided for European recovery, all of which will greatly relieve our shortage of United States dollars; for it is recognized by all, I believe, that although dollars will not save the world, the world today cannot be saved without dollars. The whole free world now has its eyes on the adoption of the Marshall plan, opposed to which is one other plan only, namely the Molotov plan. Without the re-establishment of economic health and vigour in the free countries of Europe; without the restoration of their social and political strength, necessarily associated with economic recuperation, the prospect for free people everywhere to find peace with justice, well being, and security for themselves and their children, will be gravely prejudiced; and by corollary, so will economic health and vigour in our country.
1 his endeavour of the new world to help the old is neither sure nor easy. The plan has rightly been called "a calculated risk." Already, within the last few days, it has been forcibly brought home to us and to the whole free world that political sabotage and communistic activities are rampant against the realization of the recovery of Europe. Last week, as we all know, was an intensely drastic week in history, when the tempo of the struggle over Europe was vastly and suddenly stepped up. Swiftly last Wednesday Czechoslovakia fell under complete communist control. Two days later there were signs that Finland might be next. Since last summer the communist drive has resulted in the following countries now being or about to come under complete communistic control: Poland, Augoslavia, Roumania, Hungary, Bulgaria, Albania, Czechoslovakia and Finland. These countries represent a total area of 565,000 square miles, with a total population of 100.000,000. So that today in Europe the population is divided in this way; the population of Russia in Europe and satellite eoun-' tries, 268,000,000; the population in the European recovery program area, 264,000,000.
Czechoslovakia has served the world as a laboratory for a test as to whether or not communism and democracy can govern together in the same state and participate in the direction of the same society. The destruction of democracy has been the result of the. experiment. On Thursday of last week the United States, Britain and France issued a joint statement, as follows:
By means of a crisis artificially and deliberately instigated, the use of certain methods already tested in other places has permitted the suspension of the free exercise of parliamentary institutions and the establishment of a disguised dictatorship of a single party. The consequences can only be disastrous for the Czechoslovak people.
Then a few days ago Anthony Eden, deputy leader of the opposition in Britain, and a former foreign secretary, had this to say:
What is really required is immediate positive action on our own account. If the policy of a western union is to be fully effective it must be one of mutual assistance covering economic and political fields.
Recently Senator Arthur Vandenberg, chairman of the United States foreign relations committee, set March 15 as the target date for the acceptance of the Marshall plan, adding:
The decision which must now be made is whether we shall continue to achieve our goal: the establishment of a stable world with free political institutions and the rule of law. World stability and European stability are inseparable; free institutions and genuine independence cannot perish in Europe and be secure in the rest of the world.
The Address-Air. Blanchette

I have cited these declarations, Mr. Speaker, to show in what a precarious position all free countries find themselves today, whether in the old world or the new. Therefore it would appear to me that we in Canada should be on our guard at all times against any action which might be interpreted by some as undermining constitutional authority. I heartily endorse the excellent remarks made last week by the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene), whom I see in his seat at the moment, and trust that others will weigh the portent of his speech. Freedom of speech and freedom to criticize in a democracy do not carry with them the licence to represent constituted authority as public enemy No. 1.
Again, all governments, whether municipal, provincial or federal, should do their utmost to establish economic and social security. As far as the economic field is concerned, the world is passing through such an intensive transition that it behooves all of us to be on the alert not only for the maintenance of our present living standards but for their improve-'ment- when occasion arises and it is possible to do so. In the social realm Canada has to its credit unemployment insurance, old age pensions, pensions for the blind, pensions to veterans and widows and family allocations. But it would appear to me that there is one gap in our social legislation, which is created by the lack of assistance to persons who are physically unfit to earn their living, and this irrespective of their age; young people who are invalids, older invalids who are middle aged or too young to qualify for the old age pension. Two years ago the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand) introduced a resolution advocating assistance to these people; the resolution was introduced again this year; and I trust that, when possible, the government will do its utmost to come to the assistance of such people, who are greatly in need of state help, as a worthy measure of social security.
It is to be regretted that with respect to further social measures, as planned in the dominion-provincial program by this government, certain provinces have seen fit to refuse the plan on the ground of autonomy, when autonomy was never to be violated since it was recognized that a central government can only be as strong as ithe individual provinces maintain their respective autonomy. It is all very well to make general statements by way of attacks against provincial autonomy; but I still have to hear, as far as Quebec is concerned, in what specific case or cases its autonomy was violated. The suggestion made some time ago by the federal government that old age pensions be paid needy

persons at sixty-five years of age was a proposal which certainly would have alleviated many cases of hardship and misery throughout the country. In my humble opinion the payment of old age pensions at sixty-five to needy persons, and the payment of pensions to crippled or unassisted persons unable to earn their living because of permanent physical disability, are the two most important social measures which should receive the attention of the government at the earliest possible opportunity. I sincerely trust that this government will do its utmost to assist in bringing security, both economic and social, to those two categories of needy citizens of Canada.
It was through the efforts of a Liberal administration that in 1926 the Old Age Pensions Act was passed, under which to date some $132 million has been distributed in the province of Quebec. In that province the blind have received pensions totalling $5,000,000. Together these two items amount to $137 million, of which the federal government has paid $103 million. In 1943 I had the honour to introduce in this house a resolution in favour of family allocations, which measure was placed in our statutes.
Since July 1, 1945, payments totalling $221 million have been made to Quebec, and each month 465,000 Quebec families are now receiving this assistance to help provide their children with better food, clothing and medical care, and with increased opportunities for training and education. To date, family allowances have brought to the province of Quebec a total in excess of $324 million and the other provinces have shared proportionately in this measure.
When the measure of family allocations was first brought up, we recall that, for one, the present Premier of Quebec castigated this proposal as one affecting autonomy, which argument, however, soon became on his part one of tautology.
Humanitarian and effective measures of economy to increase the security and wellbeing of our citizens represent Canada's answer to communism and other isms which rise in materialism, and thrive on misery, disorder and revolution if necessary.
No time more than the present holds more promise for the free nations of the world; and yet no time more than the present demands sagacity, judgment, experience in international affairs and the keeping of the peace in a changing civilization in both domestic and international affairs, if these same free nations of the world are to survive.

The Address-Mr. Lockhart
Mr. NORMAN J. M. LOCKHART (Lincoln): Mr. Speaker, I desire to associate myself with much of what was said by the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Blanchette). His comprehensive review of world conditions is something to which I believe we can all subscribe. I noted that the hon. member referred particularly to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent). I thought perhaps he might have included some other ministers in his eulogies, because I do not think it is fair to single out one aspirant for leadership without giving an equal chance to the others. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) would seem to run a very close second, with perhaps the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) trailing along a little bit in the rear.
I should like also to associate myself with what was said by the hon. member respecting communistic tendencies. May I, in a word, offer a tribute to the immigration officials who at this time are trying to sift the wheat from the chaff in Europe. I am sure each member in the house will extend to them his best wishes for success in their efforts. I do not know of any task which could be given any group of public officials more difficult than would be that of trying to keep out of this Canada of ours those having undesirable tendencies.
I noted the hon. member's reference to health services, and I should hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare would pay close attention to the speech delivered this afternoon by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), and that the hon. member's speech may register with the minister. May I express the pious hope that we may not have to wait until just prior to a general election to have in Canada proper health measures, as happened in connection with the baby bonus bill?
I have noted that it is the tendency of most hon. members to discuss matters having particular reference to their own constituencies, and with that in mind I propose to deal briefly with the constituency of Lincoln. This debate would appear to be the sounding board through which hon. members may place on record the merits of their particular constituencies. I am particularly favoured in that the historic county of Lincoln needs no advertising in the House of Commons, nor does the garden city of St. Catharines located in the very heart of that county.
It is a byword that over a hundred years ago that great and fertile area of Lincoln county, in which is situated the garden city of Canada, was the cradle of democratic governmentand that at a time long before confederation. In old Upper Canada it was in what was then known as Newark, now Niagara-on-the-Lake. that government in Upper Canada was born. The names of Secord, Service, Chrysler, Butler and many others stand out preeminently in Canadian history. This area was the scene of battles in the war of 1812-14. It was in this district that the battles of Queenston Heights, Lundy's Lane and Beaver Dam were fought, battles which did so much to stem the tide of the irresponsible government then threatening our future. I say, therefore, that Lincoln county forms a most important part in the history of Canada, not only in early days but at the present time.
When one passes on to those more important matters with which the people of my constituency are concerned he finds that the housing problem becomes of first importance. This afternoon I shall be content to try to reflect some of the utterances one hears when at week ends he is privileged to visit his home.
I should like to pass on to the house some of the criticisms heard. Strong criticism is made respecting the diversion of essential building materials to non-essential buildings, and the consequent neglect to have those materials made available for housing. Many of the complaints come from veterans. I have made a careful inspection of some of these complaints and I say without hesitation that the veterans in particular, if not the citizens at large, are justified in the criticisms they make.
I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) to a situation that exists in my constituency. Yesterday the minister stated that the situation prevailing in the Braefoot subdivision in British Columbia would be referred to a parliamentary committee. This committee has not yet been set up and the government does not seem to be in any hurry to set it up. It is not necessary to refer the matter I have in mind to a committee. I hope that I can make the situation so clear to the minister that he will not require to do anything but take action.
If the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) were in the house at the moment I would suggest to him that he pay close attention to the situation which exists in Niagara Falls and Welland, two progressive cities in his constituency. I think he would find that certain discrepancies exist in connection with Veterans Land Act houses there and he would be well advised to check those particular developments.
I want to direct the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs to the conditions
The Address-Mr. Lockhart

that exist in connection with a group of veterans' houses which were built in the vicinity of St. Catharines. The former minister of veterans affairs knew all about this situation because I brought it to his attention well over a year ago. He stated in the house that these houses would be put in first-class condition and that the taxpayers would foot the bill, and he suggested that the cost may be in the neighbourhood of SI,000,000. It will be interesting to follow this through to the end. I have been watching the progress being made in this one small subdivision and I shall be interested in getting figures of the complete cost a little later on. I want to commend the former minister for really attempting to put these houses in fair condition at considerable expense. There has been some improvement in the original set-up.
I would say to the present minister that the condition in connection with septic tanks is still abominable. All last summer they were digging up these septic tanks. A week ago I was in one house which has a sump pump in the basement, and the stench-I cannot call it anything else-that arose from the hole in which the pump sits was such that I would not think any person could live in the house. I am not trying to raise an issue that has no foundation. The condition that exists indicates clearly to me that the water pumped out of the sump goes into the ground and probably absorbs part of the pollution from the septic tank which is only twenty feet away. It probably joins with the liquid from the septic tank, then flows back through the weeping tile into the sump again, and there you have a perpetual motion.
I say to the minister that proper drainage beds must be provided. This thing will have to be approached in a scientific way.
Last summer they had professors from the agricultural college out there as well as other technical men, but the condition still exists. The former minister wrote to me saying that these veterans would not have to sign contracts until these conditions were rectified. Then one, two or three days after the first septic tank was dug up, representatives of the Department of Veterans Affairs were on the doorsteps of these veterans demanding that they sign contracts.
I say to the minister that that kind of thing is breaking faith with the veterans. Some of them signed because they felt they were more or less coerced into doing so. The interior painting, the exterior painting and other things had been taken care of and they felt that they might sign. They now find that their protection has been more or less taken 
away because their septic tanks are not in proper condition and they have signed contracts at increased prices. As I say, the former minister said in this house that the added cost would not be a tax on these veterans homes. I want a statement from the minister in due course as to the increased prices which have been put into some of the new contracts. I cannot accept any evasion in this matter.
Having brought this matter to the attention of the minister, I hope that he will proceed to have it cleared up, not when the veterans affairs committee is set up but immediately. The moment spring breaks, this putrid and polluted condition will reappear as it did last summer -when the stench was simply unbearable. These veterans cannot put up with it for another summer season.
I want to pass along to something that has been of particular interest to me ever since I have been in this house. I have listened to our friends of the C.C.F. and our friends of the Social Credit group who have spoken about the development of our oil resources. I have watched the type of fuel that comes from the United States. Those of us who have anything to do with the distribution of fuel sometimes think it is just the screenings, what might be swept up off the floor. Yet this type of fuel is selling today at very high prices, anywhere from $19 to $20 a ton. Its value is much less than in former days. Oil prices, too, are continually rising, and if somebody shuts off the tap in the United States we shall be in a pretty fine pickle here in Canada. Not a day passes but we hear about the shortage of electric power, and the provincial governments are struggling to cope with that shortage. We hear of blackouts; I think we have had one or two electric power blackouts in the city of Ottawa. In view of all these circumstances I ask the government: When, oh when, are you going to wake up to the necessity of formulating a national fuel, oil and power policy in ' this country?
During the war days the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) talked about what would happen in the reconstruction period. But here we are, going on year in and year out, with a shortage of coal, oil, and electric power, and the government putting up with it. We have been told over and over again that we have in Canada all these resources at our very fingertips and that all that is needed is a policy to develop them. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am in sympathy with the members of the Social Credit group who have urged year after year that our oil resources be developed. They were developed to a certain extent to meet an emergency that arose during

The Address-Mr. Lockhart
the war, but I am told that all that equipment has been dismantled and scrapped. Again I urge the government, with all the power I possess, to formulate a real fuel, oil and electric energy policy for this country. Ever since I have been in this house I have heard the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) describing the surveys that he has made of our fuel, water and power resources and detailing the wonderful possibilities for their development. I bring that to the attention of the government, which I think has been very remiss in not assuring the people of this country that something will be done in this regard.
I find in my constituency terrific criticism of the cost of government. I received a letter not long ago asking me the number of personnel in the government service. I could only write back and say that there were 69.000 more than there were before the war. The people back home just cannot understand why this terrific expense continues. They want to know when it will cease. Immediately they cast reflections on the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) for continuing the eight per cent sales tax and the twenty-five per cent excise tax on washing machines and refrigerators that the veteran needs to furnish his home. The tax is off again, on again, so that the veteran is just about fit to be tied. It is just about time that we got down to knowing where these people are and where they are not.
I know of three veterans who are building small homes. They have calculated the percentage of their gratuities and re-establishment credits that is absorbed by taxes of this type, and I warn the Minister of Finance that if he does not change the situation he will hear a protest, the like of which he has never heard before, against government policy, particularly as it applies to the veteran and the household equipment he has to buy.
Further, if the Minister of Finance does not take steps to enable the owner of a home, particularly the veteran, to get possession of his property, he will hear plenty from that quarter. I appreciate that there is a shortage of houses; nevertheless present regulations are causing hardship to the veterans, who are being done a grave injustice as I view the situation after careful investigation of all these circumstances.

of the advantages of that part of the Dominion of Canada which I have the privilege of representing. I thought that perhaps in fairness to him I might have taken the rest of my time to inform him, but I realize that I have but a few minutes at my disposal and therefore I propose to spend an entire evening with him sometime in order that I may properly inform him. Apparently he is the only one who does not know. He comes from a very remote part of the country and I shall make it my business on another occasion and in a more advantageous way to tell him all about that part of Canada which I represent. An hon. member to my right suggests that I might take him home on a week end. Perhaps it would take a whole week end to describe adequately the garden of Canada, the garden city of St. Catharines and all that goes with it.

During the few minutes at my disposal I wish to bring one important matter to the attention of the government. I desire to say something on behalf of the forty odd flying clubs at present operating in Canada who are finding it very difficult to carry on their operations. I have no wish to deal at too great a length with the subject, but I should like to go back to the year 1935 or perhaps shortly before that. It was at that time that I first discovered and observed what the few flying clubs then in existence were actually accomplishing in the development of aeronautics. I also discovered at that time the extent of the help that came from enthusiastic citizens, men of means, men of vision, who saw the necessities of the future.
Air training was just beginning to grip the imagination of our youth. In my own city, as I recall, when the one-seater Moth planes used to fly overhead the boys of those days gazed in amazement and wonder. I say it is well that those flying clubs assumed the responsibility they did. As I remember, the department of civil aviation lent some aid. In my own city, the city council gave financial assistance. But the greatest contribution in those days came, in my opinion, from the young men themselves, young men who almost denied themselves the necessities of life in order to equip themselves so that they might reach their objective, which was to become air pilots.
The Address-Mr. Lockhart

About that time war clouds began* to descend. They were hovering overhead, and there were many misgivings not only in government circles but on the part of the people generally who began to wonder what was in the offing. Airports began to grow up. Perhaps behind the scenes there was an influence of which some of us knew little.
As one looks back over those twelve or fifteen years, I think we have to express thanks, yes, to Providence, Mr. Speaker, that those things did* happen and that our people were becoming air-minded. I recall with considerable pride the time when one class of candidates graduated from our small flying school. I believe there were fifteen of them. One or two, because of vision and other difficulties, took up ground work and technical work.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, those were important diays and they meant much to us in the years that followed. Then the darker days came. Britain was attacked. Our boys who had received their pilots licences, and those who had learned ground-crew work, technicians in large numbers from my own particular area, went in defence of Britain to help her in her dilemma. A great many of those young men- and I am sure that what is true of my area is true of many other parts of Canada-went over and joined the Royal Air Force. Canada owes a great debt of gratitude to those young men, because many of them never returned and never had an opportunity even of transferring to their own R.C.A.F.
This was before the commonwealth air training scheme was mooted. There have been many criticisms about delay in connection with that scheme, and I will not go into that tonight, though it is a story in itself. But I say that none were more critical than those young pilots whose ambitions were being thwarted to some extent.
Then the war clouds broke. The government finally took action, and I say that the accomplishment of our youth is one of the proud spots in Canada's contribution to the war.
About that time elementary schools began to grow throughout the dominion. Elementary No. 9 was established in my area and a subsidy was paid by the government for every pilot who graduated from those different schools.
I want to pause, Mr. Speaker, to say just a word to those public-spirited citizens who put up the large sums of money required by the government before an elementary school could be started. I wish to pay a word of tribute to many real citizens across this country who made those schools possible. As

I recall it, although I am subject to correction, $35,000 was the sum which had to be put up. In connection with elementary school No. 9 in Lincoln county, I want to say that the money was given without interest and was given wholeheartedly. I am quite sure that not one cent of interest was ever collected by those men who put up the large contribution which made possible the establishment of our elementary school.
The war was won and the R.C.A.F. played an important part. The forty odd airports in Canada are now trying to carry on alone. The government seems to have lost interest in them.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AFFECTING MEMBERS' TRANSPORTATION -WIVES AND DEPENDENT MEMBERS OF FAMILIES
speechtext: They have lost all interest.

maintopic: QUESTIONS AFFECTING MEMBERS' TRANSPORTATION -WIVES AND DEPENDENT MEMBERS OF FAMILIES
speechtext:
Financial help is being curtailed. As I understand it, the subsidy has been stopped. Consequently these flying clubs are finding it difficult to carry on. They are faced with increasing cost of gasoline, maintenance and parts. Everything is costing a great deal more than it did prior to and during the war. The grim part of it all is that on March 2, 1948, the war clouds are again appearing distinctly on the horizon. In spite of the experience we had, and in spite of the sacrifice of thousands of young men who gave their best-and the government needed their help badly-these flying clubs are being left to fight their own battle.
In conclusion, I wish to urge the government to get behind these forty odd flying clubs. I want the government to impress upon these clubs the fact that their efforts have been and are now being appreciated. I want the government to help these clubs for at least one year. They are the nucleus of an organization, the need of which none of us knows how soon may again arise. A year's procrastination might prove disastrous. I urge the government to increase their interest and not decrease it. I was in consultation with one member of the executive of the flying club in my own area and he expressed willingness to submit to the government their figures on costs, and any information that the government requires; but, as one of the senior officers of the local flying clubs, he pleaded that the government show more interest in their work. A new generation of youth is still being thrilled by even the Moth plane that flies overhead. So I again make an urgent appeal. The world picture is not too reassuring. With all the persuasiveness that I possess, I ask the government to keep our pilots in the air. We dare not do otherwise in the light of events in the world today.

The Address-Mr. Knowles

maintopic: QUESTIONS AFFECTING MEMBERS' TRANSPORTATION -WIVES AND DEPENDENT MEMBERS OF FAMILIES
speechtext:
I propose to address my remarks tonight, Mr. Speaker, to one general subject, namely, the older citizens of this country, with particular reference to their need for, and their undoubted right to, old age security. At the outset I want to say that in my view living conditions in Canada, on the average, are unquestionably better than they are in many other parts of the world. That, of course, is a somewhat comforting thought to those in Canada who enjoy the average standard of living, and it is a very comforting thought to those who enjoy a standard of living above the average. But my concern, and I think it should be the concern of all members of parliament, is with those who live at a standard below the Canadian average, and there are millions of them in this country. As I see it, it is a sad commentary on the government and its supporters that they spend so much time in boasting of the standard of living in Canada and fail to recognize the stark tragedy of insecurity which faces millions of our people. I could speak tonight of wage earners who, week after week, take home $10, $15 or $20 less than is necessary to provide their families with a proper standard of living. I could talk of housewives trying their best to buy sufficient food out of the money that is available to them for that purpose. I could speak of the plight of parents who see the family allowance that was given to them a few years ago wiped out by the increased1 cost of living. I could speak of housing conditions, of doctors' and hospital bills that mortgage the future of a great many of our people, to say nothing of the failure thus far to prepare adequately for the health of all Canadians along the lines suggested this afternoon by my good friend the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair). But I have chosen, as I have already indicated, to confine my remarks tonight to the insecurity of old age in Canada.
I now want to confront the house with the fact that this problem of old age insecurity is not only one which should concern us right now in the month of March, 1948, on behalf of the old people now with us in this country, but is one which will become more serious as time moves on. In the face of that, I submit that if we are worth our salt as public representatives we must come to grips with this problem in a much more effective and satisfactory manner than has vet been done.
A moment ago when I said this problem would get worse I overheard someone to my right ask why. Well, I have here the answer, in some information which I have secured from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. First,
this page of figures gives a breakdown of the Canadian population by age groups for each ten-year period from 1851 to 1941. According to these figures, in 1851 only 2-7 per cent of the Canadian people were sixty-five years of age and over; -but that percentage has increased every ten years since then, until in 1941, 6-7 per cent of the Canadian population was sixty-five years of age or over. The increase has been not only in percentage terms but also in absolute figures. That increase took place at the general rate during the ten years between the last two censuses. In 1931, according to these figures, 5-6 per cent of our people were sixty-five years of age or over, and the number was 575,830. In 1941, as I have said- already, the percentage was 6-7, and the number was 767,815.
This table indicates that there has been a similar increase, both in percentage terms and in absolute figures, in those between the ages of twenty and sixty-four. In 1851 some 41 per cent of our people were in that age bracket. In 1941 the percentage was 55-8 between the ages of twenty and sixty-four. Obviously there must have been a percentage decline somewhere to account for the percentage increases in these upper age brackets, and that percentage decline has taken place in the age group zero to nineteen. In 1851 some 56-3 per cent of the Canadian people were nineteen years of age or under, while in 1941 that percentage was only 37-5. In other words, we in Canada are an aging population.
In addition to the set of figures to which I have already referred-, I hold in my hand a copy of bulletin No. 4, issued by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics in 1946, entitled, "The Future Population of Canada." This is indeed an excellent piece of work, which provides a great deal of useful information. On page 30 of the booklet I find a table which points out that in 1971 our population of sixty-five years of age and over, which in 1941 numbered 767,815, will be 1,523,000. In other words, by 1971 our population of sixty-five years of age and over will be in absolute terms, just about double what it was in 1941. At that time our people sixty-five years of age and over, instead of being 6-7 per cent of the population as was the case in 1941, will constitute 10-4 per cent of the Canadian population.
I submit that these estimates in regard to the future population of Canada-and they are official estimates from- the Dominion Bureau of Statistics-highlight the fact that the problem of old age security is one that we must tackle with a great deal more determination than has yet been shown by the government of the day. This afternoon I asked a question T have asked many times before in this house,
The Address-Mr. Knowles

as to when we might expect an improved old age pension plan. Of course I was given the stock answer that government policy will be made known in due course. I suggest that the situation is bad enough today, when 6-7 per cent of our people are sixty-five years of age and over. Today's provisions will not at all fill the bill twenty-three years from now, when 10-4 per cent of our population will be in that age bracket.
There are those whose reaction to these figures will be that this increase in the percentage of people sixty-five years of age and over might be counterbalanced by a decline in the percentage of those younger, which some would say might provide more room for employment for older people than is the case today. Entirely apart from my own objection to that idea, my own feeling that when people reach that age they are entitled to retirement, in any civilized society, there are two facts which speak against it. On the one hand, there is the fact of the technological improvements that are taking place all the time. The other reason is the one to which I have already referred, namely, that there is also taking place an increase both in the percentage and in the absolute number of Canadians between the ages of twenty and sixty-four, with a particular increase shown in the group around forty-five and fifty.
Just incidentally I remind hon. members that people in this age group are already having unemployment problems of their own. That is something else with which we must concern ourselves, in addition to old age security; that is, the rights in our society of those in the age group forty-five to fifty and fifty-five. The figures on page 29 of the booklet to which I have already referred indicate that at the same time as there is this increase in the percentage of those sixty-five and over, there will be an increase in the percentage of those between forty-five and sixty-four. Thus the problem of finding something for the older people to do wall not be solved by any lessening of those in the next younger group.
But may I suggest that the fact to which I have just called attention, namely, the parallel increase in the percentage of those in the working years, is not only a difficulty; it also provides an opportunity for the development of an economy that will provide better old age security. The simple fact is that if there are more people available for work in the ages from twenty to sixty-four, or take any section of that bracket you wish, it means it is possible to produce, with the working force we will have, sufficient wealth to provide security for our old people, as well as proper care

and maintenance and education for the children of the land. And may I suggest that this idea, while it is my own, is supported by conclusions to which the Dominion Bureau of
Statistics comes in bulletin No. F-4. I wish time would permit me to read more, but I shall limit myself to just a few sentences. On page 31, I find this:
Secondly, the proportion of children in the population begins to decline in the period 19411971, while the proportion of old people continues to rise. The former decreases more rapidly than the latter increases so that the trend for the period is toward a state of lighter dependency.
And note this sentence:
This trend, together with the increase of productive workers, suggests that the burden of dependency will be spread over a greater number of people, and hence the effect of an increase ini the aged population rvith the heavier burden which it entails will not be so costly a problem per capita.
In other words, this situation I have presented, which might strike some hon. members as something of a problem, is looked upon by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics as creating a situation in which we can do a better job toward providing old age security, because of the increased number of workers in the working ages which we shall have in this country.
Not only does the Dominion Bureau of Statistics point to the possibility of this sort of thing being done, but it urges that it must be done; for on the same page I read this:
The trend toward an increasing proportion of old people in the population implies intensification of the problems of the aged. The emphasis upon change and the depreciation of tradition prevalent in modern industrial society, and the social structure which such a society engenders have placed the aged in a precarious economic and social position in which more of the responsibility for their welfare is being of necessity assumed by the state.
Then the bureau goes on to say something I like very much. It points out that not only is there the necessity of greater social security for older people being provided by the state, but that we must begin to give thought to the position of older people in our society. In other w'ords, they will not be satisfied just with being the recipients of an adequate old age pension, if that means being put on the shelf. The paragraph concludes with this sentence:
More thought will probably be given in the future not only to the problem of widening state services for the aged but also to careful consideration of the whole position of the aged in North American society.
I commend that to the house, not just as an academic study but as a suggestion that

maintopic: QUESTIONS AFFECTING MEMBERS' TRANSPORTATION -WIVES AND DEPENDENT MEMBERS OF FAMILIES

speechtext:
The Address-Mr. Knowles
this indeed is a problem about which we should be concerning ourselves now in 19-18, and not waiting until 1971 arrives.
With regard to the present, the staggering fact is that, even with the means test restrictions at present attached to our old age pension legislation, a tremendous percentage of the Canadian people over the age of seventy are able to qualify for the old age pension. In 1941 there were 460,091 Canadians seventy years of age or over. I find that 186,863 of them, or 40-6 per cent, were on old age pensions. This indicates that 40-6 per cent of Canadians in 1941 over seventy years of age were sufficiently destitute to qualify for old age pensions.
The figure of 186,863 in 1941 had risen to 215,889 as at September 30, 1947. I have been unable to get the exact figure as to the total number of Canadians in 1947 aged seventy and over. But by doing a bit of simple interpolating I find that the same percentage of roughly 40 per cent of Canadians at the age of seventy are qualifying for the old age pension. May I point out also that the figure 186,863 in 1941, which was 40-6 per cent of the people over seventy, was 1-7 per cent of the Canadian population as a whole.
Again, if we look to the future, in 1970 Canadians seventy years of age and over- and I take my figures from the same booklet -will number 955,000. If by any chance the qualifying age for old age pensions is still seventy in 1970-and heaven forbid-then 40 per cent of that population seventy years and over will be 382,000 persons, or 2-8 per cent of the estimated population in 1970 of roughly 14,000,000.
I have also a figure in this connection which relates to 1971. I take these figures according to the statistics that are available. I now take the age of sixty-five and over in the hope that surely by 1971, even if this government is still in power, the qualifying age for the old age pension will have been brought down to sixty-five. It ought to be that right away for men, and sixty for women.
But let us assume for statistical purposes that the qualifying age is sixty-five in 1971. If that is so, there will be in that year 1,523,000 persons who are sixty-five years of age and over; and if 40 per cent of them qualify the number will be 609,200, or four per cent of the total population, which it is expected will be 14,600,000.
I have given these figures, at the risk of confusing the house with so many of them, to point up the statement I made some minutes ago that the problem of old age insecurity as it is today, or old age security
as it should be, is one to which we should give our attention, both because of the plight, of the old people in this month of March, 1948, and because if we are worth our salt as members of parliament we should be laying a proper foundation for the future life of this country.
I was led to look up these figures because of references made to them in the past by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martini, and by his predecessor, who produced figures from the same source to argue with us in this group that our demands for old age pensions of $50 a month at age sixty-five v-ere impossible to meet now, and would be still more impossible to meet a few years hence, because of the increase in percentage of old people.
I submit that an honest facing of economic facts, and a courageous facing of our responsibilities as members of parliament, leads us not to be frightened by figures like this, but to accept them as a tremendous challenge and opportunity. I must remind the house that, after all, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics is not concerned about philosophy or politics, or anything other than just plain hard facts; yet it comes to the two-point conclusion: (al that something more must be done for the old people, and (b) that something more can be done, because there will be a larger working force in the ages around forty, fifty, and fifty-five.
I have made fairly abundant references to these tables. So far as my argument is concerned, all the figures I wish to give I have now presented to the house, and I am not asking that these tables be put on the record for my purposes. So far as I am concerned, my argument at this point is complete. I feel, however, that these figures as to changing percentages of population with respect to ages in both the past and the future, and figures with respect to the working force in the next twenty-three years are valuable and would be useful to lion, members and to those who read Hansard for reference purposes. For that reason I suggest that the house might give its consent to the tables being placed on record.

I move on to suggest that parliament must begin to think pretty seriously about this whole problem right away. One thing that we must try to resolve is this question of contributory or non-contributory old age pensions. No one can deny that it is impossible to think of making the present pension contributory or of attaching any contribution as a necessary part of the pension which people are now receiving or which people of fifty-five,
sixty and sixty-five years of age will be receiving in due course. That phase of the matter has to be looked at by itself.
There is beginning to develop an opinion in Canada, in the trade union movement for example, that so far as younger Canadians are concerned it would be a good idea to have some kind of contributory plan started now; with individuals, industry and the government all taking part; the whole thought being that
18D2
The Address-Mr. Knowles

it will not be satisfactory to wake up in 1971 to discover that the problem has become a much larger one and that we had not made plans for it back in 1948. When you start to talk about a contributory plan I say that you must keep separate the case of those on the present inadequate old age pension and you must realize also that any proper social security plan must be an over-all plan.
It is no good having a contributory scheme for old age pensions here, a contributory scheme for health insurance there and a contributory scheme for unemployment insurance some place else, and have other schemes as well which fail to interlock. The result is that the cost becomes prohibitive and the benefits inadequate. If we can get going with an over-all scheme it would be possible at reasonable cost to provide security in that way and also to remove any question as to the rights of people to these benefits. Despite all the boasting that hon, members opposite like to do, the fact is that we in Canada are far behind in the matter of an over-all social security plan.
I want to point out that that is not the only side of the picture. One must not think we are going to provide an adequate old age security plan in 1971 simply by having a contributory plan started now. What is really required to have adequate old age security is to have a planned economy that accepts it as proper that one section of the community, namely the children, are cared for with respect to all their needs, their wants and their rights out of the whole national wealth and similarly that another section of the community, namely those of sixty, sixty-five years and up, are equally well provided for out of the current production at the time the people are at those ages. We have already had experience with superannuation benefits of one kind and another completely losing their value because of the change in the value of money, and we know also that the standard of living changes as decades come and go. Here is hoping that our standard of living will go up in the next few decades. Old age security in 1971 must not be security in terms of what we think would be sufficient in 1948; it must be related to economic conditions of that time. So I submit that this calls not only for having some kind of a contributory plan started now, one which does not require contributions of those who are at present receiving old age pensions or who are near to receiving them, but also for economic planning which includes an overall social security arrangement.

By all means. The provinces have to be human if this government is not.
My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), dealt with a problem last night which both he and I have raised in this house a number of times, the plight of superannuated civil servants. The figures my colleague gave last night underlined the seriousness of their problem. I shall not take time to repeat those figures or to give similar ones, but may I say that I, too, was bitterly disappointed when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), after all the promises we had last year from him to give consideration to this matter, announced on January 23 of this year:
While it is recognized that superannuated civil servants encounter difficulties during periods of rising costs, these are similar to the difficulties faced by other retired persons living on pensions, annuities or other savings, and the government does not consider that it would be fair or proper in these circumstances to single out its former employees for special assistance.
That is an argument which looks at three people, A, B and C, all starving, and says: We are sorry that we cannot do anything for A and B, so it would not be fair to them for us to keep C alive. So far as we are concerned, that is not a satisfactory answer.
I have here a specific case of a retired civil servant in the city of Winnipeg who is also a veteran of the first world war. Had he not earned a civil service pension of $58.85 a month-that is all he is getting and he is one
of the favoured ones-he points out that he could now qualify for a burnt-out pension of $60.83; or, if not that, he could qualify for an old age pension of $60 a month for himself and his wife. Here are three different superannuation amounts that he might have qualified for, but he can only draw one, and that happens to be his civil service superannuation of $58.85 a month. That individual case epitomizes the unfairness that exists with respect to all these three groups, old age pensioners, superannuated civil servants and burnt-out veterans. Had time permitted, I would have gone in more detail into the plight of burnt-out veterans; but, as time is short, I just add my plea to the government to bring in that legislation soon and to make the increase much larger than has been indicated thus far and to grant a reasonable increase also to the widows of the non-pen-sioned veterans, who thus far are still getting only $30.41 a month-a disgrace to this country.

I refer to the retired employees of the Canadian National Railways, and the Canadian Pacific non-pensioned employees about whom I have spoken so often. Incidentally, the other day the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), answering the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), said that in view of the government's answer that it could not do anything for superannuated civil servants, he felt it would not be fair for him to ask the Canadian National Railways to increase the retirement benefits of their employees, even those receiving only the basic $25 a month. So there you have the government saying that not only C shall starve but B too. The government should be giving a lead in these matters, instead of using the fact that others are not doing anything as an excuse for inaction on their part.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your generosity and I hope that the house will realize that, although democracy calls for many other things as well, at the very least it must provide security for our old people, and sooner or later that includes us all.

Mr. Speaker, it had not been my intention to participate in this debate, but during the course of the debate there have arisen in my constituency some problems which, although having a
1S04
The Address-Mr. Brown

local aspect, do affect the national economy. There have also been referred to in this debate, some matters which affect my constituency and on which I should like to make some comment.
But may I first offer my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Dion) and the seconder (Mr. Dickey) of the address. It may be we have by this time forgotten that of which they spoke, but may I, in offering them my congratulations, state that in my humble opinion they upheld the dignity, integrity and ability of that section of the house which we affectionately call Little Chicago.
Recently a situation has arisen which has caused a shut-down of a large number of industrial plants, resulting in considerable unemployment and temporary hardships to many thousands of industrial workers. This was due to the failure of the supply of natural gas so-called, or should I say fuel gas, to meet the demand caused by the severe winter which resulted in an increased consumption by householders. I said natural gas so-called, because I understand that at the present time only about 45 per cent of the present supply can be classed as natural gas. I am informed that a great deal of our supply of gas for the Windsor area is stored in underground wells and drawn upon as the need arises, as a result of manufacturing processes at Sarnia, Ontario. We may as well, therefore, face the fact that the supply of natural gas, especially in southwestern Ontario, is rapidly being depleted. In fact, from official sources at the disposal of all members I have observed that in 1940 in the whole province of Ontario 13,000,000 cubic feet of gas were produced, which had dropped in 1946 to 6,000,000 cubic feet, while natural gas in the province of Alberta had increased from 17,000.000 million cubic feet in 1936 to over 40,000,000 cubic feet in 1946.
The city of Windsor I understand to be the largest automobile manufacturing centre in the British empire, as well as the largest pharmaceutical centre in the British Empire. We also produce a great percentage of the salt, with its by-products of chlorine, caustics and other chemicals consumed in the Dominion of Canada, so that a stoppage of activities in these industries cannot but be reflected in the economy of the whole dominion which depends so largely on the commodities we produce.
If, therefore, we are not to be able to depend on natural gas for our industrial activities during critical weather conditions it will be necessary that we take steps to provide some other fuel to be consumed. The
fMr. Brown.]
four main sources of heat generally employed either for commercial or domestic consumption, and excluding atomic energy, are coal, gas, oil and hydro-electric power.
During world war I, I am informed that, in the 'United States alone, coal furnished 80 per cent of the energy used in that country. Oil supplied 12 per. cent and the others about 4 per cent each. Since then, a tremendous change has taken place. I am now informed that, in the United States, the use of natural gas has jumped 434 per cent, oil, 413 per cent, hydro-electric power, 350 per cent, but coal consumption has risen only about 5-5 per cent.
So that it is that in 1947, it is estimated coal furnished about 47 per cent of the power' for heating in the United States; oil supplied about 30 per cent; natural gas 12 per cent, and hydro-electric power 11 per cent. It would therefore seem that a continuing increase in the demand for oil and gas in this country as well as in the United States would be inevitable. We have huge supplies of natural gas as well as coal in Alberta, but because of the long distance there is no means, in southwestern Ontario especially, of tapping these supplies. On the other hand, we have supplies of coal in the maritime provinces and in the western provinces, but by reason of the long haul these do not stand competition with United States producers.
It is further estimated that on the basis of the current production the supply of crude oil is calculated to last about ten or eleven years at today's accelerated consumption pace. Further, we cannot look too hopefully to a longterm supply of crude oil. Natural gas, on the other hand, is estimated to have a lifetime of about thirty-three years. There appears, however, to be a sufficient supply of coal, anthracite, bituminous and lignite, for many years to come.
It is, therefore, necessary for us to take stock and lay long-term plans to meet the demands of liquid or gas fuel. In the United States the secretary of the interior has obtained an appropriation of $9 billion for a synthetic oil program, to study ways and means of converting natural gas into synthetic gasoline and diesel oil as a short-term program, and later to convert coal to oil or gas as a long-term program. The transition to a synthetic era will doubtless come as needed and be spurred on or retarded by developments in technology and more knowledge of atomic energy, or by the discovery of more oil resources.
I am informed that the most promising solution of the short-term program is the production of gasoline and diesel oil from

The Address-Mr. Brown
natural gas. The Standard Oil Development Company recently dedicated a research laboratory at Baton Rouge, Louisiana, which will work with the pilot plants in that area now producing petroleum products, gas and oil. Other plants are now planned in Texas and Kansas.
We have in the city of Windsor and environs facilities to produce annually a surplus of an estimated three and a half billion cubic feet of coke-oven gas, which would contribute largely to the supply of fuel gas in the highly industrialized area of southwestern Ontario for all time to come. This could be produced if the blast furnaces now erected on the Dominion Steel property at Ojibway, adjacent to the city of Windsor, were put into operation. This property is situated on one of the finest inland waterways in the world. It has excellent harbour facilities, highway facilities, and every other essential for the successful operation of a steel plant, which is so vital to the expanding economy of the dominion.
May I, therefore, urge the government to take every step possible in seeing that all the possibilities of this project, on which so many hundreds of thousands of dollars have been expended, is utilized to the fullest extent, to the benefit not only of the city of Windsor, but of the whole Dominion of Canada in making accessible these basic products which are so badly needed.
May I further urge the government to make such appropriations as are necessary to explore the possibilities of converting the vast supplies of natural gas into gasoline and oil and of converting coal into oil, not only as a means of satisfying domestic consumption for peacetime activities but as a further means of national defence. This, as I have stated, is being carried on in the United States and was done successfully in Germany and other countries, and Canada takes second place to no country in national research.
There is another matter which I should like to deal with briefly since it is wholly within my constituency, a matter which I have been dealing with since the summer of 1946. It has to do with the veterans land project known as the Roseland farm sub-division and the Oliver farm sub-division. My interest in this matter has been to see that these veterans, who have fought and bled and suffered for us' should now be rehabilitated in an atmosphere of industry, contentment and security, that they be re-established in our community where they may rear their children in an atmosphere of peace and quietness, and till their gardens, deriving therefrom as much satisfaction as is humanly possible. It is my hope that these 5849-115
veterans may continue to enter into the life of the community, socially, economically and politically, to the fullest extent.
I do not propose to thresh old straw from which all the wheat has been removed. Suffice it to say that I propose to continue, to the best of my ability, to serve the people of these sub-divisions as my constituents. The Roseland sub-division is probably one of the most beautiful locations for such a project to be found anywhere. This sub-division is approximately two miles from the business area of the city of Windsor. It has winding drives, small and neat white homes which circle a nine-hole golf course, well treed and with well kept greens and fairways. The possibilities of improvement of this sub-division cannot be reckoned, for it is an area in which any veteran may be proud to live. The Oliver farm sub-division, which is a short distance away and on the same highway, is a more recently developed project which also has winding drives and is easily accessible to the main part of the city by two highways. It is also in close proximity to another golf course.
It is regrettable, however, that these two sub-divisions are not serviced by a school, particularly a school which would accommodate the very small pupils. The township, by reason of its financial position, is not able to finance a school building for these areas, and the federal authorities have no jurisdiction in educational matters.
I personally accompanied the township representatives and the representatives of the Department of Veterans Affairs, including the trustees of the township of Sandwich West school board, who have been doing such a magnificent job, in waiting upon the Premier of Ontario and other officials of that governmental body. It is to be hoped that some provision will soon be made, by the authorities having jurisdiction, to provide some accommodation at an early day. I might state that the Veterans Land Act administration has already indicated that it will provide the land at any time for a school, at no charge.
The hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy), however, has raised a point on which I think I should make some comment, for he has stated, at page 1209 of Hansard the following. I do not propose to read all of it, but in referring to a committee which was formed for the purpose of seeing that the veterans were getting fair value for their money he has this to say, in part:
The valuations that were made by this committee were made last December.
Further on:
I regret to say this, but it is nevertheless necessary that I should, because the minister in
The Address-Mr. Brown

his statement emphasized that the valuators bad never seen the prices previously quoted by the Veterans Land Act administration.
Then a little further on he says:
I must also refer briefly to some two or three of the valuations of the Windsor area rather than give the figures. The information is available in the report which the minister tabled. On >a great many of the houses there was a difference of only a few dollars, $10, $12, $15 and $25 which would) indicate to me, or to anyone else, that this committee certainly must have bad this report, because it is almost physically and mentally impossible for valuators to valuate one hundred houses and come within $10, $15, $20 or $25 of the price which the government had set as the price to the veterans.
There is, of course, no reference there to the fact that this committee also found on other houses prices differentiating to the extent of about SI ,000; that is to say, the price on the house as set by the Veterans Land Act administration was reduced by nearly $1,000. I am not sure whether the hon. member, in making the remarks, intended them as a reflection upon the members of this committee who, not being members of this house, are not here to defend themselves. But since I had a great deal to do with influencing the government in appointing this committee, I should like to make some comment thereon. Mr. J. E. L. Price, who was chairman of the committee, is of Montreal. He had been unknown to me except by reputation which, I might state, was very high. Mr. Price, however, is chairman of the Canadian Legion national housing committee, and has probably done more, as a private individual, for the housing of veterans than any other person in Canada. Furthermore, I am willing to accept the advice of the Canadian Legion as to his integrity, ability and reputation. I, however, know the other two members of the committee who made the valuation on the Windsor houses and have known them for many years. These men were picked because of their outstanding ability in their respective fields, their reputations for fairness and integrity, and certainly because of no political affiliation; for none of these three gentlemen, to say the least, has been known as a member of the political party to which I adhere.
I attended the opening sessions of this committee and accompanied them on part of their inspection; and whenever any suggestion of any price was mentioned, they were vigorous in their rejection of any such assistance. All these gentlemen are returned soldiers themselves and interested in veterans' activities; and through you, Mr. Speaker, I want to express to them my gratitude for the work

which they undertook solely as a public service in seeing that the veteran obtained full value for his money.
There is another item which I should like to mention briefly in conclusion, and it has to do with a class of persons who are not in this house and who are not in a position to defend themselves. Of course I realize that, from a political point of view, it is never profitable to defend civil servants. But I hear from time to time many stories as to the operation of various departments. One story which obtained considerable publicity and notoriety had to do with the customs officials in my constituency. It appeared that at one time there had crossed at Windsor a car which contained an invalid who was returning from a hospital where she had undergone an operation. These people-and I believe there were three of them-when asked if they had anything to declare, said, "We have some gifts in the trunk". The examiner went to the trunk and tore the claws off (he fur and damaged the car, so it was reported. Then the officer is reported to have made them move the lady, who was an invalid, inside the customs house where she was kept for quite a while. The officer also is reported to have said, "You did not tell us about this item and that item". And the reply was, "I told you that we had gifts, and the names are on them". That might be misleading because the true facts of the case are as follows. Upon being requested to declare any goods to customs, they mentioned a few groceries and some small Christmas gifts which they had been given at Christmas and were now bringing into Canada. Their baggage was brought into the office and examined by a female examiner who found several articles of new clothing. As each article was found, one lady remarked, "My sister gave me that for my daughter-in-law," and each such item was allowed entry. These consisted of several articles, including a cotton playsuit, a pair of shoes the lady was wearing, a pair of shoes the gentleman was wearing and other small articles, although these were not packaged as gifts. On examining the automobile three children's dresses, two small lamps, and two pairs of ladies' shoes were found in the trunk of the car, and these goods still had the price tags attached. While they were also stated to be gifts from friends in the United States, after further questioning one lady admitted she had purchased them herself in the United States. Upon further search of the automobile, one carton of cigarettes was found concealed in a bag of groceries, and six cartons of cigarettes were found under the

The Address-Mr. Brown
front seat. These were placed under seizure because no declaration had been made.
On other occasions we have also been told that it would be advisable or expeditious to hold sort of sales or educational meetings with the examiners located at the border in order to attempt to turn them into diplomatic policemen. It is reported that the one making the statement had noticed quite a few oases at the border where examiners became rough and tough. I feel sure that the hon. member for London (Mr. Manross), who is such a congenial member of this house, never meant any offence to these public servants, and I am sure that he with his charming personality has had no difficulty personally. But his remarks, if hon. members wish to look them up, may be found at page 1157 of Hansard. You know, Mr. Speaker, I have found that these men referred to as the examiners usually treat a traveller somewhat in the same manner as the traveller treats the examiner. I do not deny that because of the imposition of the restrictions as of November 17, when no advice was given to the officers, nor could it be given to them, many assumed their responsibilities conscientiously. Many were new men who had been taken on without instruction. It is only fair to say, however, that these officers, most of whom had been recently released from the armed services, were and are trying to do a job conscientiously and efficiently. I too realize that these officers are salesmen for the Dominion of Canada; and since they have a valuable and serviceable product to sell I know they will do a good job. We as civilians can be of immeasurable assistance to them in trying to make their job, which in itself may be unpleasant, a cheerful and pleasant experience, if we realize the tension under which they are working and are willing to co-operate with them to the fullest extent. I have always found that if I approached these officers with a smile and showed courtesy and consideration, I received similar treatment from them, and vice versa.
So, if the department decides to hold these sales or educational meetings, as suggested by the hon. member, let us not restrict them to customs or immigration officers. Let all the citizens of Canada be invited to participate, to show the world we can live in unity, industry and prosperity.
